notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered.

---

# 1 Kings 22:1–26 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — "Then three years passed without war between Aram and Israel."

**Traditional Reading:**
- These three years are reckoned from the peace Ahab made with Ben-Hadad in 1 Kings 20:34. Gill notes they were not three full years but parts of years, and the three-year respite for Ahab is thought by some Jewish commentators to be due to his (shallow) repentance in 1 Kings 21:27–29 — God delayed the threatened judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Barnes adds that the Assyrian threat under Shalmaneser III may have united Israel and Syria temporarily during this period. Ahab and Ben-Hadad apparently fought together at the Battle of Qarqar (853 BC). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_kings/22.htm)
- Precept Austin notes that Ahab had a golden opportunity to defeat Syria in 1 Kings 20 but failed; now his failure would "come back to haunt him like a boomerang." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary)

**Modern Scholarship:**
- The IVP Background Commentary (cited by Precept Austin) notes Shalmaneser III's records list "Ahab of Israel" among the coalition that fought Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC. The success of this coalition likely emboldened Ahab to move against Aram for Ramoth-Gilead. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary)

---

## v. 2 — "However, in the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to visit the king of Israel."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill notes the distance from Jerusalem to Samaria was about 32–40 miles. Jehoshaphat came to visit Ahab, probably after the marriage alliance between Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram and Ahab's daughter Athaliah (2 Kings 8:18). Ahab entertained him lavishly (2 Chronicles 18:1–2). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Precept Austin reads "came down" both geographically (Jerusalem is elevated) and spiritually: "he has 'come down' spiritually!" It calls this "another good man corrupted by a wicked woman." The marriage alliance led to compromise. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary)
- Ellicott adds that this is the first time since 1 Kings 15:24 that the history of Judah is touched upon in Kings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-22.html)

---

## v. 3 — "…Do you not know that Ramoth-gilead is ours, but we have failed to take it from the hand of the king of Aram?"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ramoth-Gilead was a Levitical city of refuge in the territory of Gad (Joshua 20:8; 21:38), under Solomon's administration (1 Kings 4:13). Ben-Hadad had promised to return Israelite cities (1 Kings 20:34) but failed to return this strategically vital one. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)
- Precept Austin, citing Dale Ralph Davis, notes the economic motive: Ramoth-Gilead sat on the King's Highway, and "incense and spice caravans trucked through" — whoever controlled it collected customs tolls. "It's a shame to have a turnpike running through a place if you aren't sitting in the toll booth." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary)

---

## v. 4 — "So he asked Jehoshaphat, 'Will you go with me to fight against Ramoth-gilead?' Jehoshaphat answered … 'I am like you, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Ahab wisely recognised his own forces were insufficient, so he sought Jehoshaphat as an ally, leveraging the marriage tie. Jehoshaphat's reply pledged full military support. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word notes the city was only about 40 miles from Jerusalem, making Jehoshaphat's involvement somewhat logical from a defensive standpoint. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)
- Precept Austin strongly criticises Jehoshaphat, calling this an "unequal yoke" (2 Corinthians 6:14): "Jehoshaphat who had the temple of God was choosing to agree with an idolater." It notes that "one compromise often leads to another" — the marriage compromise led to the battle compromise. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary)

---

## v. 5 — "But Jehoshaphat also said … 'Please inquire first for the word of the LORD.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Barnes calls this "characteristic piety" — Jehoshaphat, a godly king, took advantage of his position to insist on seeking Yahweh before going to war. He asked it be done "today" so Ahab could not postpone. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_kings/22.htm)
- Gill: Jehoshaphat, "being a pious and religious prince, did not choose to go into a war at once, without consulting the Lord by his prophets." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word calls this a "bold request" given the adversarial relationship between Ahab and Yahweh's prophets. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 6 — "So the king of Israel assembled the prophets, about four hundred men … 'Go up,' they replied, 'and the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill identifies these as false prophets — possibly the prophets of the groves who ate at Jezebel's table (cf. 1 Kings 18:19), since the number (400) matches. He notes their words are "very ambiguous, like the oracles of the Heathens" — they do not specify who or what would be delivered, or to which king. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Barnes argues these were "the prophets attached to the worship of the calves; not real prophets of Yahweh." He notes they used "Adonai" rather than "Yahweh" (the Hebrew word differs in v. 6), suggesting they shrank from using the covenant name until they saw Jehoshaphat insisted on it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_kings/22.htm)
- The Church Pulpit Commentary: "Ahab welcomed the four hundred because he knew exactly what the four hundred would say." Ahab's disposition was "a willingness to welcome religion, if religion will only sanction the views, projects, and passions of its patrons." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/1-kings-22.html)

---

## v. 7 — "But Jehoshaphat asked, 'Is there not still a prophet of the LORD here of whom we can inquire?'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Jehoshaphat suspected these were false prophets, though he would not directly call them so, to avoid affronting Ahab. He asked diplomatically if there were any other prophet of the Lord. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Barnes: Jehoshaphat was "dissatisfied" — these men were creatures of Ahab, tainted with calf-worship if not Baal-worship, and had promised victory but not convincingly in the name of Yahweh. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_kings/22.htm)

---

## v. 8 — "…'There is still one man who can ask the LORD, but I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad. He is Micaiah son of Imlah.' 'The king should not say that!' Jehoshaphat replied."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill notes Micaiah is thought to be the same unnamed prophet from 1 Kings 20:35–43 who had prophesied that Ahab's life would go for Ben-Hadad's. Ahab hated him because of that last message. Jehoshaphat replied "very modestly, though perhaps too gently" that prophets of the Lord should be respected whatever their message. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Ellicott confirms Josephus's tradition that Micaiah was the prophet of 1 Kings 20:35–43 who had already been imprisoned by Ahab. The words of v. 26 ("return him") seem to confirm this. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word: "Ahab hated the messenger because of the message. His real conflict was with God, but he focused his hatred against the prophet Micaiah." Citing G. Campbell Morgan: "Hatred of the messenger of God is clear evidence of willful wickedness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## vv. 9–10 — "So the king of Israel called one of his officials … 'Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.' Dressed in royal attire, the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat … were sitting on their thrones at the threshing floor by the entrance of the gate of Samaria, with all the prophets prophesying before them."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Micaiah was in prison (as v. 26 shows), so Ahab knew exactly where to find him. The threshing floor at the gate was a place of judgment, where courts were held in an open space. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word: This illustrates the ancient custom of holding court at the city gates, where thrones were set up for high officials. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 11 — "Now Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made for himself iron horns and declared, 'This is what the LORD says: With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Horns were emblems of power; iron horns signified even greater strength. Zedekiah may have been alluding to the blessing of Joseph in Deuteronomy 33:17 (bullock with horns representing Ephraim and Manasseh), since Ahab ruled in the territory of Joseph's tribes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word: "This must have been a vivid and entertaining presentation. We can be certain that every eye was on Zedekiah." Yet no matter how powerful the presentation, the message was unfaithful. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 12 — "And all the prophets were prophesying the same, saying, 'Go up to Ramoth-gilead and prosper, for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Enduring Word: "It was certainly persuasive to have 400 prophets speak in agreement on one issue." The unanimity gave an appearance of divine confirmation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 13 — "Then the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah instructed him, 'Behold now, with one accord the words of the prophets are favorable to the king. So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: The messenger (possibly out of pity for Micaiah in his miserable prison condition) advised him to go along with the crowd so he might gain the king's favour and be released. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary: "How often has the same base advice been given! How often has it been followed! … One of the most difficult lessons of life is to learn to stand alone when all the prophets are prophesying falsely to please the rulers of the world." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-kings-22.html)

---

## v. 14 — "But Micaiah said, 'As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever the LORD tells me.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Micaiah swore by the living God that he would speak truly and faithfully, "keeping nothing back, nor adding anything, whether it be good or evil, pleasing or displeasing." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word notes this was a dramatic scene: "a prophet in rags and chains stand before two kings, ready to speak on behalf of the LORD." Citing Trapp: Micaiah had "lately seen the Lord sitting upon His throne… and hence he so boldly looked in the face these two kings in their majesty; for he beheld them as so many mice." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 15 — "When Micaiah arrived, the king asked him … 'Go up and triumph,' Micaiah replied, 'for the LORD will give it into the hand of the king.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott**: Micaiah spoke in "defiant irony," as "a true disciple of Elijah in the defiant irony of the tone in which he takes up and mocks the utterance of the false prophets so bitterly as at once to show Ahab his scorn of them and him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-22.html)
- **Gill**: Micaiah "answered not in the name of the Lord … nor seriously, but by way of derision; he took up the words of the prophets, and bantered them." He delivered the words "with such gestures, and such a tone, and with a contemptuous smile in his countenance, which showed that he spoke not seriously, but sarcastically." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- **Enduring Word** agrees: "his tone was probably mocking and sarcastic. He said similar words to the 400 unfaithful prophets, but delivered a completely different message." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 16 — "But the king said to him, 'How many times must I make you swear not to tell me anything but the truth in the name of the LORD?'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Ahab recognised Micaiah was not speaking in the Lord's name or seriously; the "how many times" implies Ahab had previously adjured him on other occasions, indicating a history of Micaiah faithfully delivering unwelcome truth. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary: "The 'how many times' shows how faithfully Micaiah must have fulfilled his duty of speaking messages of God to his erring king." Ahab detected the "tone of scorn which rang through the assenting words." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-kings-22.html)

---

## v. 17 — "So Micaiah declared: 'I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the LORD said, "These people have no master; let each one return home in peace."'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown): The purport is that the army of Israel would be defeated and dispersed, that Ahab would fall in battle, and the people would return home without their king. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_kings/22.htm)
- Gill adds that Jarchi (Rashi) thought only Ahab would be slain, since 1 Kings 22:31 shows the Syrians targeted only the king; the other part of the judgment from 1 Kings 20:42 ("thy people for his people") was deferred. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word: "Micaiah was challenged to tell the truth, and now he changed his tone from mocking to serious." The shepherd imagery pointed to the death of the leader. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 18 — "Then the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, 'Did I not tell you that he never prophesies good for me, but only bad?'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Enduring Word: "King Ahab said that he wanted the truth — but he couldn't handle the truth. What he didn't consider was that though Micaiah prophesied evil towards Ahab, he prophesied truth." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)
- Gill: Ahab attributed Micaiah's prophecy to "spite and malice" and personal hatred, not to the Lord, and therefore argued it should not be regarded. He noted that Micaiah's earlier prophecy three years prior had not yet come true, so he dismissed this one too. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)

---

## vv. 19–23 — The Vision of the Heavenly Council and the Lying Spirit

### v. 19 — "I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: This is represented "as in a vision, in which things are brought down to the capacities of men, and not as really transacted." The scene mirrors the earthly court — Ahab and Jehoshaphat on their thrones — but "a far greater King, even the King of kings, and in a more splendid manner." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Ellicott: This recalls Job 1:6–12 and the "intercourse of Satan with the Lord Himself." The vision is "to be taken as a symbol, and nothing more. (Josephus, characteristically enough, omits it altogether.)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-22.html)
- Enduring Word: Since the right hand is the place of favour, this may indicate God spoke to the combined host of heaven, "both faithful and fallen angelic beings." It notes the reality that Satan and fallen angels have access to heaven (Job 1:6, Revelation 12:10). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

### vv. 20–22 — The Divine Council and the Volunteering Spirit

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Pulpit Commentary**: God's question "Who shall persuade Ahab?" means "Ahab's death in battle had been decreed in the counsels of God, and … Divine Wisdom had devised means for accomplishing His purpose." The "spirit" (Hebrew: *the* spirit) is understood by many modern commentators (Thenius, Keil, Bähr) as "the spirit of prophecy" personified — "the power which, going forth from God and taking possession of a man, makes him a prophet." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-22.html)
- **Gill** identifies the spirit as "the evil spirit, Satan, the father of lies, the old deceiver, who came forth from his own place and his own company." He rejects the Jewish tradition that it was the spirit of Naboth seeking revenge. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- **Enduring Word**: The spirit was "one of the fallen angels" who volunteered. "Since Ahab wanted to be deceived, God would give him what He wanted, using a willing fallen angel who worked through willing unfaithful prophets." It cites D.J. Wiseman: "It is rather a personified spirit of prophecy … It represents the power of a lie in the mouth of someone opposed to the truth." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

### v. 23 — "'So you see, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the LORD has pronounced disaster against you.'"

**This verse is the most theologically debated in the passage.**

**Traditional/Reformed Reading (God's Sovereignty over Deception as Judgment):**
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The difficulty — that the Almighty appears to sanction lying — "vanishes if we remember that this is anthropopathic language, and is merely meant to convey that God had 'taken the house of Israel in their own heart' (Ezekiel 14:5). Ahab wished to be guided by false prophets, and the justice of God decreed that he should be guided by them to his ruin. Sin is punished by sin." It calls this the *lex talionis* — Ahab chose lying instead of truth, so by lying he would be destroyed. The difficulty is "that of the permission of evil in the world; of the use of existent evil by God to accomplish His purposes of good." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-22.html)
- **Gill**: "The Lord hath put a lying spirit in the mouths … that is, suffered the lying spirit to suggest a lie to them, and sent them strong delusions to believe that lie, whose minds were disposed at any rate to flatter Ahab." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)

**Reformed (Ligonier):**
- "While the Lord does not Himself lie, He can send others to deceive people. … When people persistently oppose the truth, He will hand them over to a lie, hardening them in their sin (Rom. 1:18–32). Ahab did not want to obey the truth, so the Lord sent him a lie." (from search excerpt; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lying-spirit-from-the-lord)

**Baptist/Reformed (John Piper, Desiring God):**
- "God does ordain that lying happen as part of his judgment on the guilty." God never lies, but "governs all things in the universe, including the sins of sinful men. Sin does not cease to be sin because God governs it and guides it for the good of his people and the glory of his name." The same principle applies to Joseph's brothers' sin and Judas's betrayal. "God is able to superintend a thousand circumstances and influences so that a sinful prophet will think a lie, without God himself lying." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/does-god-lie)

**Evangelical (GotQuestions):**
- The article notes Ahab had "declared war on God by killing His prophets," so God brought judgment through a lying spirit. God did not Himself lie but used a deceiving spirit to accomplish His righteous judgment on a king who refused the truth. (from search excerpt; https://www.gotquestions.org/lying-spirit.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):**
- Focuses on the spiritual realm reality: the lying spirit was a fallen angel operating through false prophets. "Since Ahab wanted to be deceived, God would give him what He wanted." Also notes that some well-intentioned teaching denies Satan can be in God's presence, but this passage (along with Job 1 and Revelation 12) shows otherwise. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## v. 24 — "Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah went up, struck Micaiah in the face, and demanded, 'Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Zedekiah acted "in contempt of him, and to show his indignation." He struck Micaiah in open court before two kings, presuming Ahab would protect him. His question was a boast — he claimed to have the Spirit and could not imagine it leaving him for Micaiah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Barnes: Micaiah's hands were probably bound (since he came from prison), making him defenceless. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_kings/22.htm)
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary calls this "the syllogism of violence." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-kings-22.html)

---

## v. 25 — "Micaiah replied, 'You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: Zedekiah would either flee from battle or hide in Samaria from the populace who would blame him and the other prophets for Ahab's death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Barnes: "When the news of Ahab's death, caused by his following thy counsels, reaches Samaria, and thou hast to hide thyself from the vengeance of Ahaziah or Jezebel, then, in that day, thou wilt know whether I or thou be the true prophet." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_kings/22.htm)
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary: "If the hands of the prophet were bound as he came from the prison, there would have been an infinite dignity in that calm rebuke." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-kings-22.html)

---

## v. 26 — "And the king of Israel declared, 'Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill: The word "return him" confirms Micaiah had been in prison before. "Amon the governor" was the chief magistrate under the king, a sort of sheriff in charge of the prison system. "Joash the king's son" was likely not a literal son but a state officer — perhaps the viceroy or head of the royal household while the king was away at war. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-22.html)
- Barnes similarly treats "the king's son" as a state office rather than a literal son, comparing 2 Chronicles 28:7. The governor of the city had control of the public prison. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_kings/22.htm)
- Enduring Word: Ahab "responded the way many tyrants do when they are confronted with the truth." Micaiah was returned to prison and deprived (bread and water of affliction, v. 27). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/)

---

## Summary of Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**The key theological divergence is over vv. 19–23 — the lying spirit.**

| Tradition | Emphasis | Source |
|-----------|----------|--------|
| **Reformed** (Ligonier) | God's absolute sovereignty: God sends deception as judicial hardening on those who persistently reject truth. God Himself does not lie but uses secondary agents. | https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lying-spirit-from-the-lord |
| **Baptist/Reformed** (Piper, Desiring God) | God "ordains that lying happen as part of his judgment." God governs all things including sinful acts without Himself sinning. | https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/does-god-lie |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word) | Emphasises the reality of the spiritual realm — fallen angels in God's presence, spiritual warfare behind earthly events. The spirit is a fallen angel. | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/ |
| **Older Evangelical** (Pulpit, Gill) | The language is anthropopathic. God permits rather than directly causes; it is the *lex talionis* — Ahab chose lies, so lies destroyed him. | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-22.html |
| **Lutheran** | Not found in searches of LCMS.org or 1517.org. | — |
| **Methodist/Wesleyan** | Not found in searches of wesley.nnu.edu or seedbed.com. | — |
| **Catholic/Orthodox** | Not found within search limits. | — |

**On other verses**, the traditions are broadly agreed: Micaiah is the faithful lone prophet; the 400 are false prophets (whether Baal prophets, calf-worship prophets, or compromised Yahweh prophets); Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab was a spiritually dangerous compromise; and Micaiah's ironic "Go and prosper" in v. 15 was sarcastic mimicry of the false prophets.
